 If you’re looking for the Connections answer for Sunday, October 25, 2026, read on—I’ll share some clues, tips, and strategies, and finally the solutions to all four categories. Along the way, I’ll explain the meanings of the trickier words and we’ll learn how everything fits together. Beware, there are spoilers below for October 25, NYT Connections #1,232! Read on if you want some hints (and then the answer) to today’s Connections game. 
 If you want an easy way to come back to our Connections hints every day, bookmark this page . (If you play Wordle or Strands , check out our hints for those games, too.) 
 Below, I’ll give you some oblique hints at today’s Connections answers. And farther down the page, I’ll reveal the themes and the answers. Scroll slowly and take just the hints you need!

 The category types in today’s Connections puzzle
 Here are spoiler-free hints that describe the type of each category in today’s Connections:
 Yellow category - Similar meaning
 Green category - Related nouns
 Blue category - Pop culture
 Purple category - Related nouns
 Hints for the themes in today’s Connections puzzle
 Here are some spoiler-free hints for the groupings in today’s Connections:
 Yellow category - What a thief or burglar does.
 Green category - You usually boil these for nine to 11 minutes, or until al dente.
 Blue category - They have the same first name.
 Purple category - These all relate to the same verb.
 BEWARE: Spoilers follow for today’s Connections puzzle!
 We’re about to give away some of the answers. Scroll slowly if you don’t want the whole thing spoiled. (The full solution is a bit further down.)
 A heads up about the tricky parts
 PALM, THUMB, ELBOW, and FINGERS all belong to separate categories today.
 Another word for BOW TIE today is “farfalle,” and it’s something you might find among the Italian food at the grocery store.
 FINGERS goes with a verb to describe an action you might do to get someone’s attention.
 What are the categories in today’s Connections?
 Yellow: STEAL
 Green: PASTA SHAPES
 Blue: FICTIONAL TOMS
 Purple: THINGS THAT CAN BE SNAPPED
 DOUBLE BEWARE: THE SOLUTION IS BELOW
 Ready to learn the answers to today’s Connections puzzle? I give them all away below.
 What are the yellow words in today’s Connections?
 The yellow grouping is considered to be the most straightforward. The theme for today’s yellow group is STEAL and the words are: BOOST, PALM, POCKET, SWIPE.
 What are the green words in today’s Connections?
 The green grouping is supposed to be the second-easiest. The theme for today’s green category is PASTA SHAPES and the words are: BOW TIE, ELBOW, SHELL, WAGON WHEEL.
 What are the blue words in today’s Connections?
 The blue grouping is the second-hardest. The theme for today’s blue category is FICTIONAL TOMS and the words are: RIPLEY, SAYWER, SWIFT, THUMB.
 What are the purple words in today’s Connections?
 The purple grouping is considered to be the hardest. The theme for today’s purple category is THINGS THAT CAN BE SNAPPED and the words are: FINGERS, FOOTBALL, GLOW STICK, RUBBER BAND.
 How I solved today’s Connections
 THUMB and SAWYER could be the last names of fictional Toms.
 I see a lot of hand anatomy words, but I think PALM goes with POCKET, SWIPE, and BOOST as words for stealing something. 🟨
 RUBBER BAND and GLOW STICK might be things you can snap or bend? Hmm.
 FINGERS is plural, but nothing else on the board is. Since PALM was in its own category separate from FINGERS, THUMB, and ELBOW, I think those latter three words are probably in their own categories, too.
 Maybe THUMB and SAWYER do go together. I think Tom RIPLEY (from The Talented Mr. Ripley ) is another fictional Tom. I’m going to assume Tom SWIFT is the last one—that feels like the most likely last name. 🟦 Yep, that works .
 What do you think so far?
 GLOW STICK, RUBBER BAND, and BOW TIE all end in words that seem vaguely related: stick, band, and tie. I guess those could all be verbs for affixing something to another thing. Maybe ELBOW (bow) also works? Let’s try. Nope! Total miss.
 ELBOW could go with a word like “tennis.” SHELL could go with a word like “turtle.” FINGERS could go with “spirit.” FOOTBALL could go with “flag” or “Sunday night.” I’m a bit lost here.
 Oh, SHELL, ELBOW, WAGON WHEEL, and BOW TIE are all pasta shapes. 🟩
 That leaves GLOW STICK, RUBBER BAND, FINGERS, and FOOTBALL. I think my first guess for GLOW STICK and RUBBER BAND as “things you can snap” is the answer here: you can snap your FINGERS and “snapping” a FOOTBALL is another word for throwing it with force or speed. 🟪

 How to play Connections
 I have a full guide to playing Connections , but here’s a refresher on the rules:
 First, find the Connections game either on the New York Times website or in their Games app (formerly the Crossword app). You’ll see a game board with 16 tiles, each with one word or phrase. Your job is to select a group of four tiles that have something in common. Often they are all the same type of thing (for example: RAIN, SLEET, HAIL, and SNOW are all types of wet weather) but sometimes there is wordplay involved (for example, BUCKET, GUEST, TOP TEN, and WISH are all types of lists : bucket list, guest list, and so on).
 Select four items and hit the Submit button. If you guessed correctly, the category and color will be revealed. (Yellow is easiest, followed by green, then blue, then purple.) If your guess was incorrect, you’ll get a chance to try again.
 You win when you’ve correctly identified all four groups. But if you make four mistakes before you finish, the game ends and the answers are revealed.
 How to win Connections
 The most important thing to know to win Connections is that the groupings are designed to be tricky. Expect to see overlapping groups. For example, one puzzle seemed to include six breakfast foods: BACON, EGG, PANCAKE, OMELET, WAFFLE, and CEREAL. But BACON turned out to be part of a group of painters along with CLOSE, MUNCH, and WHISTLER, and EGG was in a group of things that come by the dozen (along with JUROR, ROSE, and MONTH). So don’t hit “submit” until you’ve confirmed that your group of four contains only those four things.
 If you’re stuck, another strategy is to look at the words that seem to have no connection to the others. If all that comes to mind when you see WHISTLER is the painting nicknamed “Whistler’s Mother,” you might be on to something. When I solved that one, I ended up googling whether there was a painter named Close, because Close didn’t fit any of the obvious themes, either.
 Another way to win when you’re stuck is, obviously, to read a few helpful hints–which is why we share these pointers every day. Check back tomorrow for the next puzzle!
